name: Kefir (fermented milk drink)
short: ADHD trial: children on kefir self-reported more sleep problems. No kefir-related bacteraemia in 54 critically ill adults; diarrhoea in 2 on laxatives. Kefir peptides not covered.
text: These sources are about kefir, the fermented-milk drink; none of them studied kefir peptides. In a 2024 open-label phase I safety and feasibility study, kefir was given in escalating amounts to 54 critically ill adults with an intact gastrointestinal tract, who were watched for gastrointestinal symptoms; none showed signs of kefir-related bacteraemia (bacteria from the kefir in the blood), and no side effects such as bloating, vomiting or aspiration were noted, except diarrhoea in two patients who were also on laxatives. The abstract describes no comparison group. A 2023 systematic review of randomized trials of kefir taken by mouth (18 publications reporting 16 studies) found that safety was assessed in only 5 of the 18 publications and that 12 studies had a high overall risk of bias; the reviewers concluded that kefir appears to be safe for generally healthy people to consume, but that efficacy and safety data from high-quality trials are needed. In a randomized study in 15 healthy adults with lactose maldigestion, kefir and yogurt reduced the perceived severity of flatulence by 54% to 71% compared with milk, and abdominal pain and diarrhoea were negligible with all five test meals. In a 6-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in children aged 8 to 13 with ADHD (53 completed), children in the kefir group self-reported more sleep problems after the intervention than the placebo group, while movement monitors showed fewer minutes awake; gastrointestinal symptoms were a secondary outcome, and the abstract reports no other significant group differences. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
